section: Impact of GST on commerce, industry and state finances; unresolved GST issues
subsections: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs
Compensation cess end and cess for loan repayment

accepted.s: Which of the following is the most direct contribution of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) to inter-State commerce?
o: Replacement of input tax credit by a turnover tax
Creation of a common national market through tax harmonisation
Exemption of all inter-State supplies from taxation
Retention of State border check-posts for all goods
accepted.x: GST created a common national market by harmonising indirect taxation across States. It also helped reduce the cascading effect through input tax credit.
accepted.tq: Identify the core objective rather than choosing an extreme or reversed consequence.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: An electronic document is mandatory under GST for the movement of goods whose value exceeds:
accepted.x: An e-way bill is mandatory for the movement of goods valued at more than Rs 50,000.
accepted.tq: Recall the threshold figure directly and distinguish it from nearby numerical distractors.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: For the movement of goods, an e-way bill is generally valid for:
o: One day for every 50 km
Two days for every 200 km
One day for every 200 km
One day for every 100 km
accepted.x: The validity of an e-way bill is one day for every 200 kilometres of movement.
accepted.tq: Test a specific numerical rule using close range-based alternatives.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding e-way bills:
1. Their rollout helped replace physical checks at State borders.
2. Their use contributed to a reduction in truck waiting time.
3. Their volumes increased by 21 per cent year-on-year during April–December 2025.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. E-way bills replaced physical border checks, reduced waiting time, and recorded 21 per cent year-on-year growth during April–December 2025.
accepted.tq: Combine operational effects with a current quantitative fact and test all statements together.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: The removal of inter-State check-posts after the rollout of e-way bills primarily resulted in:
o: A shift from digital to manual tax reporting
Reduced transit time and logistics costs
Higher physical verification of consignments
The abolition of input tax credit
accepted.x: The replacement of physical checks and the dismantling of border check-posts reduced truck waiting time, transit time and logistics costs.
accepted.tq: Link the administrative reform to its practical logistics outcome.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: Which of the following best indicates the expansion of formalisation under GST between 2017 and 2025?
o: The taxpayer base remained unchanged at 66.5 lakh
The taxpayer base increased from 1.51 crore to 66.5 lakh
The taxpayer base increased from 66.5 lakh to 1.51 crore
The taxpayer base declined from 1.51 crore to 66.5 lakh
accepted.x: The taxpayer base expanded from 66.5 lakh in 2017 to 1.51 crore in 2025, indicating greater formalisation.
accepted.tq: Compare the direction and magnitude of a two-point trend without reversing the figures.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: Which of the following combinations most appropriately describes the benefits of GST formalisation for small firms?
o: Restriction of procurement to intra-State suppliers
Removal of digital records and greater dependence on intermediaries
Exemption from all registration requirements and cash-only transactions
Credit eligibility and procurement parity
accepted.x: Formalisation improved credit eligibility and procurement parity for small firms. Digitisation also reduced human interface.
accepted.tq: Select the paired benefits directly associated with formalisation.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: The composition scheme is primarily intended to ease compliance for:
o: Large multinational corporations
Small taxpayers and MSMEs
Only exporters claiming refunds
Only petroleum producers
accepted.x: The composition scheme is designed to reduce the compliance burden for small taxpayers, including MSMEs.
accepted.tq: Match the simplified compliance mechanism with its intended beneficiary.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about the GST composition scheme:
1. The turnover limit is up to Rs 1.5 crore for goods.
2. The turnover limit is Rs 50 lakh for services.
3. A taxpayer under the scheme can claim input tax credit.
4. A taxpayer under the scheme can collect GST separately from the customer.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
accepted.x: The composition scheme applies up to Rs 1.5 crore for goods and Rs 50 lakh for services. Its taxpayers cannot claim input tax credit or collect tax separately.
accepted.tq: Find the two correct eligibility statements and reject the reversed features of the scheme.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: Under the composition scheme, the flat rate specified for goods and services respectively is:
o: 6 per cent for goods and 1 per cent for services
6 per cent for both goods and services
1 per cent for goods and 6 per cent for services
1 per cent for both goods and services
accepted.x: The specified flat rate is 1 per cent for goods and 6 per cent for services.
accepted.tq: Test a comparison-table row by preserving the order of the two categories.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: Which of the following is a continuing compliance burden associated with GST?
o: Complete absence of digital reporting
Abolition of automated registration
Mandatory physical border verification for every consignment
Multiple returns and input tax credit matching
accepted.x: Multiple returns and input tax credit matching remain important compliance burdens under GST.
accepted.tq: Distinguish an identified unresolved burden from benefits and abolished procedures.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: Which of the following forms part of the GST reform agenda for reducing compliance difficulties?
o: Pre-filled returns, time-bound digital registration and automated exporter refunds
Manual registration, physical returns and delayed refunds
Separate tax systems for every inter-State route
Abolition of e-invoicing and e-way bills
accepted.x: The reform agenda includes pre-filled returns, time-bound digital registration and automated refunds for exporters.
accepted.tq: Identify the complete reform package rather than a reversal of digitisation.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: GST reduced the cascading effect of taxation mainly through:
o: A tax exemption for all intermediate goods
Taxation only at the point of manufacture
Input tax credit available at every stage
Abolition of all State taxes without replacement
accepted.x: Input tax credit at every stage reduces the tax-on-tax, or cascading, effect.
accepted.tq: Connect the stated mechanism with the economic effect instead of choosing a broad exemption.
accepted.sec: Impact on commerce - logistics, checkposts, formalisation, MSMEs

accepted.s: The compensation period under GST for States formally ended in:
o: March 2026
June 2021
June 2020
June 2022
accepted.x: The GST compensation period ended in June 2022.
accepted.tq: Separate the end of the compensation period from the later continuation of the cess.
accepted.sec: Compensation cess end and cess for loan repayment

accepted.s: Why was the GST compensation cess continued after June 2022?
o: To replace input tax credit with a direct subsidy
To finance the creation of State border check-posts
To finance only export refunds
To repay back-to-back loans raised for compensation purposes
accepted.x: The cess continued to service and repay back-to-back loans raised for GST compensation.
accepted.tq: Link the continuation of a levy to its stated debt-servicing purpose.
accepted.sec: Compensation cess end and cess for loan repayment

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the GST compensation cess:
1. It continued up to March 2026 for repayment of back-to-back loans.
2. It was scrapped on 22 September 2025 except in relation to tobacco.
3. It ended on 31 March 2026.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The cess continued for loan repayment, was scrapped on 22 September 2025 except for tobacco, and ended on 31 March 2026.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the announcement date, the exception and the final cessation date.
accepted.sec: Compensation cess end and cess for loan repayment

accepted.s: The tobacco excise and Health Security and National Security Cess introduced in place of the compensation cess are:
o: Shared only with producing States
Not shared with States
Shared with States through the GST Council
Transferred exclusively to local bodies
accepted.x: The replacement levies are not shared with the States.
accepted.tq: Test the important distinction between a divisible GST-related levy and a non-shared levy.
accepted.sec: Compensation cess end and cess for loan repayment

accepted.s: In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals, the Supreme Court held that GST Council recommendations are:
o: Advisory only to the Union executive but binding on courts
Binding only on Parliament and not on States
Persuasive but not binding on Parliament and State legislatures
Binding on Parliament and State legislatures in every matter
accepted.x: The Supreme Court held that GST Council recommendations are persuasive and not binding on Parliament or State legislatures.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between persuasive and binding constitutional effects.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: The judgment in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals was delivered in:
o: May 2022
May 2023
May 2021
May 2020
accepted.x: The Mohit Minerals judgment was delivered in May 2022.
accepted.tq: Recall the year and month of a landmark ruling using close chronological distractors.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: The description of India as a “flexible federation” in the context of GST is associated with:
o: The exclusive legislative power of Parliament under Article 249
The simultaneous legislative power under Article 246A
The abolition of State legislative competence over taxation
The power of the GST Council to enact laws directly
accepted.x: The GST framework reflects simultaneous legislative power under Article 246A, contributing to the description of India as a flexible federation.
accepted.tq: Connect the constitutional concept with the specific provision and institutional arrangement.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs consists of other landmark GST rulings cited along with Mohit Minerals?
o: Safari Retreats and VKC Footsteps
Kesavananda Bharati and Minerva Mills
Puttaswamy and S.R. Bommai
Indra Sawhney and Golaknath
accepted.x: Safari Retreats and VKC Footsteps are cited along with Mohit Minerals as landmark GST rulings.
accepted.tq: Group landmark cases from the same subject area and reject unrelated constitutional cases.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: Under the GST Council voting arrangement, which of the following is correct?
o: The Centre has one-half weight and States together have one-half weight.
Each State has an equal weight and the Centre has no vote.
The Centre has one-third weight and the States together have two-thirds weight.
The Centre has two-thirds weight and States together have one-third weight.
accepted.x: The Centre has one-third of the weighted vote and the States together have two-thirds.
accepted.tq: Recall the composition of weighted voting without reversing the Centre-State shares.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: Why does the Centre have an effective veto in the GST Council?
o: Because the Centre’s one-third vote can prevent a three-fourths majority
Because the Centre has two-thirds of the weighted vote
Because State representatives cannot vote on tax matters
Because the Centre alone nominates all State members
accepted.x: Since three-fourths weighted support is required and the Centre holds one-third of the vote, the Centre can block a proposal without its support.
accepted.tq: Infer institutional power from the voting weights and decision threshold.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: Which of the following groups of petroleum products is covered by the GST law but remains outside GST taxation until a date recommended by the GST Council?
o: Crude oil, petrol, diesel, natural gas and ATF
Natural gas, electricity, alcohol, tobacco and ATF
Coal, electricity, iron ore, cement and steel
Gold, silver, diamonds, petrol and coal
accepted.x: Crude oil, petrol, high-speed diesel, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel are within the GST law but are taxed outside GST until the Council recommends a date under Article 279A(5).
accepted.tq: Test the complete list and distinguish legal inclusion from present tax treatment.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: Article 279A(5) of the Constitution is relevant to the inclusion of which category within GST taxation?
o: Customs duties
Petroleum products
Personal income
Agricultural land
accepted.x: Article 279A(5) concerns the date from which specified petroleum products may be brought within GST taxation on the GST Council’s recommendation.
accepted.tq: Match the constitutional provision with the specific unresolved GST issue.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: Bogus input tax credit claims made through fictitious transactions are commonly associated with:
o: Compensation grants
Tax harmonisation
Composition taxation
Fake invoicing
accepted.x: Fake invoicing involves bogus claims of input tax credit. E-invoicing, e-way bills and AI-based scrutiny are used to counter it.
accepted.tq: Distinguish an enforcement problem from genuine compliance and harmonisation measures.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: Which combination is used to counter fake invoicing and bogus input tax credit claims?
o: State borrowing, compensation grants and tax amnesty
E-invoicing, e-way bills and AI-based scrutiny
Physical check-posts, cash payments and manual registers
Composition levy, customs duty and export subsidy
accepted.x: E-invoicing and e-way bills, supported by AI-based scrutiny, help detect and counter bogus input tax credit claims.
accepted.tq: Select the coordinated digital enforcement tools rather than an outdated physical-control method.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: In May 2026, the Andhra Pradesh High Court held that where Central and State GST investigations overlap, the authorities must:
o: Abandon the investigation if the entity operates in more than one State
Decide inter se which authority will proceed
Transfer every case automatically to the Union Government
Both proceed simultaneously against the same entity
accepted.x: The Court held that Central and State GST authorities must decide inter se who will proceed against a common entity, thereby preventing dual action.
accepted.tq: Identify the precise institutional solution to overlapping jurisdiction.
accepted.sec: Centre-State disputes - Mohit Minerals case

accepted.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025–26, a cut in GST rates may have what effect on revenue?
o: Volume effects may offset the initial revenue loss
It necessarily eliminates all future GST revenue
It reduces transaction volumes in every sector
It affects only customs revenue and not GST revenue
accepted.x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 observed that increased volume of transactions following a rate cut may offset the associated revenue loss.
accepted.tq: Recognise the stated dynamic revenue effect instead of assuming a static tax-base response.
accepted.sec: Evaluation studies - Economic Survey, RNR

accepted.s: The gross GST collection during April–November 2019 was approximately:
o: Rs 6.75 lakh crore
Rs 8.05 lakh crore
Rs 5.05 lakh crore
Rs 10.05 lakh crore
accepted.x: Gross GST collection during April–November 2019 was Rs 8.05 lakh crore.
accepted.tq: Recall the reported aggregate using closely spaced lakh-crore alternatives.
accepted.sec: Evaluation studies - Economic Survey, RNR

accepted.s: According to the Economic Survey 2019–20, rationalisation shocks to GST rates generally raise collections for:
o: Only one week
More than two years
One to three months
Six to twelve months
accepted.x: The Economic Survey 2019–20 noted that rationalisation shocks raise collections only for about one to three months.
accepted.tq: Test the limited duration of a revenue effect against exaggerated time periods.
accepted.sec: Evaluation studies - Economic Survey, RNR

accepted.s: The approximate Revenue Neutral Rate (RNR) proposed in the 2015 debate by the Arvind Subramanian Committee was:
o: 15–15.5 per cent
8–8.5 per cent
12–12.5 per cent
10–10.5 per cent
accepted.x: The Arvind Subramanian Committee’s 2015 debate placed the approximate RNR at 15–15.5 per cent.
accepted.tq: Recall the range directly and distinguish it from lower standard-rate figures.
accepted.sec: Evaluation studies - Economic Survey, RNR
